open.text: Knowing the rules of good design gets you halfway. The other half is a process... for applying them, and for changing a design once it's live.

guess.text: Say an online store wants a database. You could just start typing tables... but then your schema is a first guess.

steps.text: Instead, ask the same questions, in order. Gather requirements. Find the entities, and their facts. Work out how they relate. Pick keys, add constraints, normalize. Then test it with real rows.

loop.text: And when a row breaks it? Loop back, and revise.

reqs.text: Step one is plain sentences. A customer places orders. A product has a name and a price. Categories group products, and a product can sit in several.

contains.text: And an order contains products, each with a quantity... and the price charged.

nouns.text: The nouns are your entities. The verbs say how they connect.

entities.text: Step two makes each noun a table: customers, products, categories, orders.

facts.text: Step three puts each fact on the thing it describes. An email describes a customer. A price describes a product.

pointer.text: And an order doesn't copy the customer's email. It points at the customer's row, so each fact lives in one place.

relate.text: Step four: how many connect to how many? One customer places many orders... and each order has exactly one customer.

pairs.text: Products and categories are many on both sides, so they meet in a table of pairs, product categories.

hidden.text: Orders and products are many to many, too. But that link has facts of its own: how many, and at what price.

items.text: So it becomes a real table, order items, one row per line on the receipt.

keys.text: Step five, keys. Order items is keyed by the pair, so the same product can't land on one order twice.

rules.text: Step six turns rules into constraints. A quantity has to be above zero, so a line for zero mugs... is refused by Postgres itself.

copy.text: Step seven, normalize: every fact in one place. Except this design copies one fact, on purpose.

then.text: Products holds the price today. Order items holds the price charged, back then.

mug.text: Ana bought two mugs at ten dollars. The mug costs twelve now.

history.text: Total her order from its lines, and it's forty-four dollars, what she paid. Total it from today's prices, and it says forty-eight. History would quietly rewrite itself.

review.text: That's step eight: walk real rows through the design, and see what breaks.

change.text: But a design is never done. A task tracker starts with just tasks. Then people want due dates. Then projects, labels, a history.

kinds.text: That's not failure. It's the product learning about the world.

risky.text: The catch? A live schema has rows, code, reports and tests leaning on its shape... and people's habits, too.

priority.text: Say every task now needs a priority. Add it as required, in one step... and Postgres refuses.

why.text: The tasks already there have no priority, so the rule would be broken the moment it existed.

safe.text: So go in steps. Add the column empty. Backfill the old rows, here with normal. Check that none is missing. Then make it required.

means.text: That backfill is a design decision, by the way. It says what the old rows MEAN.

expand.text: Bigger changes work the same way. Say a task's one owner has to become a team of assignees.

widen.text: First, expand: add the new table beside the old column, so both shapes work.

move.text: Move the data across, then the code.

contract.text: Only once nothing reads the old column... contract, and remove it.
